title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life

references.label: NCERT Physics Part II, Class 12 — Nuclei

summary: Unstable nuclei spontaneously transform into more stable ones by emitting radiation, at a rate that follows an exponential decay law characterized by a constant half-life.
explanation: Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of any single nucleus, but for a large sample it follows a precise statistical law: the number of undecayed nuclei decreases exponentially with time. The half-life is the time required for exactly half of a given sample to decay — this value is constant for a given isotope regardless of the sample's size or how much has already decayed, which is a defining and often counterintuitive feature of exponential decay.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a sample is 'completely gone' after two half-lives — it's actually reduced to one quarter, since decay is exponential, not linear, and technically never reaches exactly zero.
Thinking half-life changes as a sample ages or as more of it decays — it is a fixed property of the isotope.
examples: Carbon-14 dating relies on its known, fixed half-life (~5,730 years) to estimate the age of organic remains.
genZNote: Half-life is the ultimate 'it's not you, it's just probability' — no nucleus knows when it'll decay, but the group behavior is completely predictable.
